pass_rule: all core questions substantially correct in the learner's own words; stretch questions inform the grade, not the gate

questions.prompt: Authentication and authorization are separate concerns in this service. What does each one answer, and how do their failures differ?
expected_points: authentication answers who the caller is; authorization answers what they may do
an authentication failure is loud — people are locked out and report it immediately
an authorization failure is silent: everything works, and everyone can see everyone's data until someone outside notices
the split shows up in the status codes: 401 means unauthenticated, 403 means authenticated but refused
the authn middleware only annotates the request; every rejection comes from the authz layer, so there is one gate to audit

questions.prompt: Describe the RBAC model you implemented: what does a Rule hold, what is the lookup, and what does the indirection through roles buy you?
expected_points: users get roles, roles carry permissions — one indirection instead of per-user grants
rules are data keyed by action: which roles may act, whether ownership is required, which roles are exempt
the lookup is a checked map read — a missing rule is a denial, not a skipped check
handlers name actions, never roles, so policy changes without touching handlers
the whole access model is reviewable on one screen

questions.prompt: When would you reach for ABAC over RBAC, and what does the extra expressiveness cost? Where does the ownership rule you wrote sit on that spectrum?
expected_points: RBAC decides from who the subject is; ABAC decides from attributes of subject, resource, and environment
ownership is already an attribute rule — comparing subject.UserID to resource.OwnerID cannot be expressed in roles
ABAC costs reviewability (predicates instead of a table), testability (combinatorial instead of finite), and easy listing filters
sensible default: RBAC spine plus a small closed set of named relationship rules; full ABAC when rules genuinely vary with the data (tenancy, classification, per-record sharing)
do not build a general policy engine speculatively

questions.prompt: A teammate ships a new route and forgets to add a policy rule for its action. What happens in your service, and why is that the behavior you want?
expected_points: no rule matches, so the decision is deny — everyone gets 403, admins included
the forgotten case is the one that ships; deny-by-default makes it a bug report instead of an open endpoint
the same rule applies to missing information: an ownership rule with no resource supplied denies rather than assumes
the only way out of Check with allow is an explicit, reasoned grant

questions.prompt: Why is the route-level check middleware rather than the first line of each handler, and what makes it impossible to register a route without a check?
expected_points: middleware runs before the handler, so a denied request never enters handler code and cannot half-execute
a first-line check is one someone can forget, and forgetting is invisible
the route table binds a pattern to an action, so registering a route means naming an action
a forgotten action is the zero Action, which has no rule and is therefore denied

questions.prompt: Bob has a valid session and the editor role. Walk me through what stops him from updating alice's document, and what would happen if only the route gate existed.
expected_points: the route gate approves the role but cannot know the owner — the document is not loaded yet
the handler loads the document and asks the policy again with the resource in hand; owner mismatch denies
with only the route gate, changing the id in the URL returns or edits someone else's object — that is IDOR
the check must sit after the load and before any decode, write, or response
listings need the same decision per row, and ownership on create comes from the session, never the request body

questions.prompt: Why does the policy return a reason alongside the boolean, and why does the reason never appear in the response body?
expected_points: tests can assert the request was denied for the expected reason — the same 403 can hide very different bugs
operators can answer 'why was this refused?' from a log query
allows and denials are both audited, at the enforcement points, so Check stays pure
telling the client 'not owner' confirms the object exists and belongs to someone else

questions.prompt: Your service answers 403 for another user's document and 404 for one that does not exist. What does that leak, and what would you change if the resource were sensitive?
expected_points: the difference is an existence oracle: an attacker can enumerate which ids are real
answering 404 for both hides existence, at the cost of confusing legitimate users and support
the trade-off is per resource sensitivity, decided deliberately
it is a one-line change because the denial response is written in exactly one place
